**Three commits** on `feature/independent-cloudflare-sandbox`, reviewing
and correcting the round immediately before this one (`d153259`/`ad26080`,
the "lease protection, owner isolation, safe Retry, atomic persistence"
round):

- **`adac6f2`** -- the main fix: conflicting meeting/Calendar
  transitions, silent intent loss on read failures, the real-entry-point
  test suite, and the prepared (not applied) Staging repair migration.
- **`f704cc8`** -- CI caught a real regression in `adac6f2` itself within
  minutes (see below) -- fixed before this branch's own CI went green.
- **`917442e`** -- CI then caught a test-only bug (not a production
  issue) in the new test file's own identity-transport helper -- fixed.

This sequence -- write, push, CI fails, fix, push, CI fails differently,
fix, push, CI passes -- is recorded in full, not cleaned up into a single
commit, because it is itself part of the evidence this round's own
instruction asked for: real CI results, actually inspected, not assumed.

### 1. Conflicting meeting/Calendar transitions -- the exact reproduction, fixed

**Independently reproduced, exactly as described**: an enrolled, present
calendar link; `scheduleProspectMeeting` reads it as present and starts
building a reschedule; a competing cancellation commits first (flipping
`desired_state` to `absent`); the reschedule's own (now-stale) batch
still runs. **Confirmed the bug was real**: the batch's own calendar
statement correctly matched zero rows (its guard failing), but the
`interactions`/`trip_prospects` statements in the SAME batch had NO
precondition tied to the calendar read at all -- they committed
unconditionally regardless. Final state: FOS said "meeting scheduled";
the calendar intent stayed "absent." Last round's own "atomic" framing
was wrong about what it actually guaranteed -- it made the BATCH
atomic (D1's own all-or-nothing commit), not the LOGICAL transition
(a guarded statement matching zero rows is not a batch failure).

**Fixed**: `trip-calendar-sync.ts`'s new `planTripMeetingScheduledIntent`
makes the same enroll/reschedule/reopen dispatch decision as before, but
now ALSO returns a `D1CrossTableGuard` -- a boolean SQL fragment
(`` `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM calendar_event_links WHERE interaction_id = ?
AND desired_state = 'present')` `` for reschedule, the absent+generation
form for reopen, `NOT EXISTS (...)` for a first-time enroll) re-verified
FRESH at execution time. `scheduleProspectMeeting` ANDs this into its OWN
`interactions` upsert's `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE` clause and its
`trip_prospects` UPDATE's `WHERE` clause too, so every statement in the
combined batch shares the IDENTICAL precondition: either all of them
affect a row together, or (the precondition went stale) none of them do
-- never the partial outcome the race used to produce. A guard mismatch
means nothing committed, so `scheduleProspectMeeting` retries the WHOLE
transition against a fresh read (bounded, `MAX_CALENDAR_INTENT_ATTEMPTS
= 5`) -- safe because nothing partial was left behind, and because
scheduling's own intent ("make this meeting scheduled at this time")
stays valid regardless of the calendar's prior state. A genuine
first-enroll race (a real `UNIQUE(interaction_id)` collision, which
rolls back the WHOLE batch including the meeting change) is caught
specifically and also retried.

**Cancellation and reopening, reviewed the same way**: `setSimpleProspectStatus`'s
cancel branch applies the identical `D1CrossTableGuard` pattern, but
checking "`trip_prospects` still has the EXACT status this request
read" -- shared across the `interactions` cancel-prefix write AND the
calendar-cancel statements. A guard mismatch there is reported as a
conflict, never retried (cancellation's own intent -- "decline a
meeting that really is still scheduled" -- is conditional, unlike
scheduling's). Reopening is already covered by `scheduleProspectMeeting`'s
own retry loop (reopen is one of its three dispatch branches); the
core's own existing "reuse the winning transition" idempotency
(`applyReopen`'s own generation-identity check, unchanged) still
prevents two concurrent reopen attempts from allocating two generations
for one cancellation -- proven again, through the real entry point this
time, by a dedicated regression (see below).

**A real regression in this very fix, caught by CI before merge**:
positioning the calendar-cancel statements AFTER the `trip_prospects`
update in the batch array seemed natural (matching the OLD order), but
D1 batch statements observe EARLIER statements' own writes within the
SAME batch -- by the time the calendar statements ran, `trip_prospects.status`
had ALREADY become the new status, making the guard permanently,
silently false and the calendar cancel a no-op on the ORDINARY,
non-racing path too (not merely the race case). CI's own new regression
test (`tests/trip-entrypoints-atomicity.test.mjs`) caught this
immediately -- commit `f704cc8` reorders the calendar statements to be
built and pushed BEFORE the `trip_prospects` update, so the guard
observes the pre-update status as intended. Independently re-verified
live on Staging afterward (see below): cancellation now actually
cancels the calendar intent again.

### 2. Stop silently losing Calendar intent on database read failures -- fixed

**Independently reproduced**: the two wrapper functions
(`tripCalendarScheduleStatements`/`tripCalendarCancelStatements`,
`trips-data.ts`) caught a thrown read error from the calendar builder
and returned an empty statement array -- `scheduleProspectMeeting` then
saved the meeting change and returned `{ok:true}` anyway, with the
calendar intent silently unchanged and nothing visible to any caller.

**Fixed**: neither wrapper function exists anymore. Both
`scheduleProspectMeeting` and `setSimpleProspectStatus` now call the
calendar-intent builders DIRECTLY and catch only at the point where they
decide the function's own return value: a read failure aborts that
attempt immediately with `{ok:false, reason:"calendar_unavailable"}`
BEFORE any `db.batch()` call runs at all -- the meeting change is never
saved either, satisfying "roll back the save with an actionable retry
response" by simply never making the save in the first place. A
genuine, non-constraint `db.batch()` failure (a real connectivity
problem, distinct from a benign guard mismatch) propagates rather than
being caught -- `scheduleProspectMeeting` only catches
`isUniqueConstraintViolation`, re-throwing everything else.
`StatusUpdateResult` gained two new reasons (`calendar_unavailable`,
`calendar_conflict` -- the latter for retry exhaustion), each with its
own distinct, actionable message in the route's `statusErrorResponse`
(503 and 409 respectively).

**Confirmed distinguished from "Calendar is intentionally disabled"**:
the durable calendar intent is read/built and recorded REGARDLESS of
`calendar_sync_enabled` -- that flag, and the absence of credentials,
only gate `attemptBestEffortCalendarReconcile`'s own live network
attempt, a completely separate step. No new background architecture was
added for this (no retry-queue table, no new column) -- the fix is
entirely "abort before saving, or retry the SQL transition," both using
only the D1 operations already in place.

### 3. Tests through the ACTUAL application entry points

New `tests/trip-entrypoints-atomicity.test.mjs` calls
`scheduleProspectMeeting`/`setSimpleProspectStatus`/`retryTripMeetingCalendarSync`
DIRECTLY -- never a stand-in UPDATE -- against a REAL local D1 database.
Since these functions `import { env } from "cloudflare:workers"` (a
module that only exists inside an actual Workers/vinext runtime, never
under plain Node), a new Node ESM loader hook
(`tests/fixtures/cloudflare-workers-loader.mjs`, registered via
`node:module`'s `register()`) redirects that one specifier to a mutable
stub (`tests/fixtures/fake-cloudflare-workers.mjs`) the test points at
the real local D1 binding -- the ONLY way found to exercise these exact
functions rather than a parallel reimplementation. (The loader also had
to re-implement Node's own extensionless-relative-import probing, which
a registered hook's `nextResolve` does not inherit automatically --
documented in the loader's own header; confirmed by direct, isolated
testing before relying on it.)

Covers, through the real entry points: the exact cancel/reschedule
interleaving above (converges correctly after one retry); competing
concurrent reopen attempts (exactly one generation bump across both,
confirmed); a genuine database-read failure (aborts before any save,
confirmed via direct query that nothing was created); a genuine batch
failure (propagates, never swallowed); recovery after a failed attempt
followed by a clean subsequent cancellation; calendar-disabled
scheduling (succeeds normally, intent still recorded); and, using the
existing `StatefulCalendarClient` against the SAME database a
trips-data.ts call just wrote to, persisted link/history consistency
together with simulated remote event existence -- proving the recorded
intent is genuinely actionable, not merely self-consistent bookkeeping.

## 2026-10-19 (fourth follow-up review): bind cancellation to the calendar link's own generation, not just the status label -- Staging deployed and live-verified, Google itself still unverified live

**Two commits** on `feature/independent-cloudflare-sandbox`, reviewing
and correcting `58551ef` (the round immediately before this one):

- **`7a86fd2`** -- the main fix: binds `setSimpleProspectStatus`'s
  cancellation guard to the calendar link's own `generation`, plus a
  new regression through the real entry points with a stateful
  simulated calendar.
- **`c610177`** -- CI caught a real regression in `7a86fd2` itself
  within minutes -- fixed before merge, same honest-recording practice
  as the prior round's own two self-corrections.

### The bug, exactly as reproduced

Independently reproduced the precise reported interleaving:
`setSimpleProspectStatus` reads the prospect's status
(`meeting_scheduled`) and the calendar link's state, and starts
preparing a cancellation; a competing request fully cancels that SAME
generation and reopens it as a NEW generation before the stale
request's own batch runs -- `trip_prospects.status` and the
interaction's own `source` both return to their ORIGINAL "scheduled"
values as part of that reopen; the stale cancellation then resumes.
**Confirmed**: the status-only guard added two rounds ago (`adac6f2`)
cannot distinguish these two situations -- it re-checks the SAME status
value it originally read, finds it unchanged (the reopen restored it),
and incorrectly lets the stale cancellation through, canceling the
REOPENED meeting and flagging the WRONG (new) generation for cleanup.

### The fix

`setSimpleProspectStatus` now additionally captures the calendar link's
own `generation` at the SAME moment it reads the interaction's source
(via the already-exported `getTripMeetingCalendarLink`), and extends its
existing guard with a second, self-contained clause:
`` EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM calendar_event_links WHERE interaction_id = ?
AND generation = ?) ``. This is the durable transition identity a
status label cannot provide: a status round-trips back to a prior
value; a generation never does (it only ever advances, via reopen).
Being a self-contained `EXISTS` rather than a bare `generation` column
reference, the SAME guard fragment is safe to AND onto `interactions`
and `trip_prospects` too, even though neither table has a `generation`
column of its own -- satisfying "enforce that identity across the
meeting, prospect, Calendar intent, and cleanup writes" with one
mechanism, not four separate ones. No change to `D1CalendarStore` or
the `D1CrossTableGuard` type itself -- only the guard
`trips-data.ts` constructs. A stale cancellation now returns
`{ok:false, reason:"conflict"}` and leaves the reopened meeting
(interaction, prospect, calendar intent, and cleanup flag) completely
untouched.

### A real regression in this very fix, caught by CI before merge

The first version of the generation guard ALSO required
`desired_state = 'present'` (to pin down the exact state, not just the
generation number). This broke the ORDINARY, non-racing cancel path:
the cancel statements this guard is applied to run in a fixed order
within the SAME batch -- the main `calendar_event_links` UPDATE (which
flips `desired_state` to `'absent'`) BEFORE the
`calendar_event_link_history` cleanup-flag UPDATE -- and D1 batch
statements observe EARLIER statements' own writes within the same
batch (the same class of self-referential-ordering bug found and fixed
two rounds ago, this time inside the NEW guard's own logic rather than
the statement ordering). By the time the cleanup statement ran, its
copy of the guard was checking `desired_state = 'present'` against a
row THAT VERY CANCELLATION had already flipped to `'absent'` moments
earlier in the SAME batch -- permanently, silently false, even with no
race at all. CI's own regression suite caught this immediately (`false
!== true` on a plain, non-racing cancel in the "competing reopen
transitions" block). **Fixed** (`c610177`) by checking `generation`
alone, dropping the self-referential `desired_state` clause: cancel
itself never changes `generation` (only reopen does), so it remains a
stable, sufficient identity across the very operation this guard
protects, and the actual race it defends against (a competing reopen
bumping `generation`) is unaffected -- a generation mismatch alone still
correctly rejects a stale cancellation.

### Regression coverage

A new block in `tests/trip-entrypoints-atomicity.test.mjs` (block 8)
reproduces the exact interleaving through the real
`scheduleProspectMeeting`/`setSimpleProspectStatus` entry points against
real local D1: schedules a meeting (generation 0); syncs it once
against a `StatefulCalendarClient` (a real simulated remote event
exists); pauses a cancellation (via the same `interceptFirstBatch`
test-side instrumentation used by earlier rounds -- never touching
production code) immediately before its own batch runs; inside that
pause, a competing request fully cancels generation 0 and reopens it as
generation 1 (confirmed via sanity-check assertions: generation 1,
`desired_state='present'`, status back to `meeting_scheduled`); resumes
the stale cancellation; confirms it returns `{ok:false,
reason:"conflict"}`; and then confirms, via direct query, that the
REOPENED meeting's own generation, `desired_state`, prospect status,
interaction source/location, AND the reopened generation's own cleanup
flag are ALL completely unaffected by the stale cancellation. Finally
reconciles against the SAME `StatefulCalendarClient` again and confirms
the real simulated event was never deleted -- the reopened meeting still
reconciles to `synced`. Every prior block in this file (lease
protection, owner isolation, the original conflicting-transition fix,
database read/batch failures, recovery, calendar-disabled scheduling,
persisted consistency, Retry) is retained and unmodified, and the
existing `tests/calendar-d1-store.test.mjs`/
`tests/calendar-adapters-integration.test.mjs`/`tests/trip-calendar-
sync-integration.test.mjs` suites are retained and unmodified.

### Checks

clean; `npx eslint .` unchanged from the documented 94-error/46-warning

## 2026-10-19 (fifth follow-up review): the Calendar schema repair rehearsed against real D1 -- the originally-proposed mechanism failed TWICE, corrected both times, now proven; NOT applied anywhere, Staging unchanged

**Scope of this round, exactly as instructed**: rehearse
`drizzle/pending-review/0049_fix_calendar_schema_text_staging_repair.sql`
against a REAL local Workers/D1 database on Linux CI, correct it if D1's
actual behavior required it, add a committed/repeatable rehearsal, and
prepare (never execute) a concrete Staging-only application plan. **Do
NOT apply the repair anywhere. Do not drop/rebuild remote tables, change
`sqlite_schema`, or touch Production. No OAuth, credentials, live Google
calls, email changes, cron activation, deployment, or merge into `main`
this round.** All of that held: nothing in this round touched Staging,
Production, or any remote database at all -- everything below ran
against an ephemeral, `persist:false`/`remoteBindings:false` local D1 on
GitHub's own Ubuntu CI runner.

### The headline finding: the originally-proposed mechanism does not work on real D1, twice, for two independent reasons

The prior round's draft used `PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF` around a
drop-and-rebuild of `calendar_event_links`/`calendar_event_link_history`,
modeled on SQLite's own documented 12-step "complex schema change"
procedure, and had only ever been tested against plain `node:sqlite` --
never real D1. This round's job was to find out whether that actually
holds up. It did not, in two separate ways, each caught by this
rehearsal's own first real-D1 CI run for that version and fixed before
the next one:

1. **`PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF` has no effect on D1 at all** (already
   suspected going into this round, per the user's own instruction not to
   rely on it) -- confirmed via research: D1 enforces foreign keys
   unconditionally on every query. The documented SQLite alternative for
   exactly this "temporarily violate an FK mid-rebuild" case is `PRAGMA
   defer_foreign_keys = on`, deferring the check to the end of the current
   transaction -- corrected to that first.
2. **`PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys = on`, inside a single `db.batch()`, ALSO
   does not reliably work on D1** -- this is the actual headline finding,
   and it would not have been caught without rehearsing against a real D1
   binding with synthetic data that genuinely exercises the FK. The first
   real-CI run of that version failed with:
   ```
   Error: D1_ERROR: Durable Object was reset and rolled back to its last
   known good state because the application left the database in a state
   where constraints were violated: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed:
   SQLITE_CONSTRAINT (extended: SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_FOREIGNKEY)
   ```
   at the `DROP TABLE calendar_event_links` step. This matches a
   confirmed, currently open/unresolved upstream limitation --
   [cloudflare/workerd#7657](https://github.com/cloudflare/workerd/issues/7657)
   and [cloudflare/workers-sdk#16071](https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/issues/16071)
   -- D1 performs its own commit-time foreign-key consistency check on a
   `db.batch()`'s Durable-Object-level storage transaction, and that check
   does not reliably honor `defer_foreign_keys`'s SQL-level deferral
   window the way plain SQLite does. **`defer_foreign_keys` is therefore
   not a dependable mechanism for this kind of rebuild on D1**, despite
   being SQLite's own documented answer to this exact scenario everywhere
   else. The repair was redesigned to never drop a table while anything
   else's FOREIGN KEY still points at it at all (rebuild the child table
   WITHOUT its FK first, then the parent, then the child again WITH the FK
   restored) -- no deferred-checking of any kind relied upon.

That redesign's own first real-CI run then caught a THIRD, independent
real-D1 quirk: it used `ALTER TABLE <temp> RENAME TO <real-name>` to move
the rebuilt table into place, and the real table's own stored schema text
came back as `CREATE TABLE "calendar_event_links" (...)` -- **double
quotes**, not the backtick quoting every committed migration actually
uses. This is a well-known SQLite behavior (`ALTER TABLE ... RENAME TO`
always re-quotes the renamed identifier with double quotes, regardless of
the original CREATE statement's quoting style) -- not a new bug, but one
that would have silently reintroduced a NEW schema/baseline mismatch
(`compareSchemaObjects()` compares stored SQL text, not just structure)
in the exact same breath as fixing the original one. **Corrected again**:
the final table under each real name is now always created by a literal,
directly-quoted `CREATE TABLE` statement -- never produced by a rename.
Only the OLD table (dropped immediately after its data is copied out) is
ever renamed, so its resulting quote style never persists anywhere.

A fourth, smaller, non-blocking finding along the way: **D1's in-Worker
`D1Database` binding (`db.prepare()`/`db.batch()`) rejects `PRAGMA
integrity_check` outright** with `D1_ERROR: not authorized: SQLITE_AUTH`
-- unrelated to the repair's correctness, but it means that specific
check can never be run directly against a live D1 binding. The wrangler
CLI's `d1 execute --remote --command` path does **not** have this
restriction (confirmed: `scripts/verify-remote-restore.mjs` already runs
`PRAGMA integrity_check` this exact way against Production's own restore
verification) -- the proposed Staging procedure below uses that path for
this specific check, never the binding.

### What finally passed, and the exact evidence

**Commit `d029060`** (branch `feature/independent-cloudflare-sandbox`) is

  realistic data; it does not prove Staging's own specific live rows

  than assuming the rehearsal's result transfers unchanged.

  "temporarily violate an FK mid-rebuild" pattern -- a genuine platform

  pattern.
- **`ALTER TABLE ... RENAME TO` permanently changes an identifier's
  quoting style to double quotes.** This is a general SQLite/D1 fact this
  round discovered, not specific to this migration -- worth remembering
  for any FUTURE schema change in this codebase that considers a
  rename-based rebuild: never let the renamed name be the one that
  persists; always create the real, final name directly.

  unverified** -- no OAuth client, no credential, no live Google API call

`scripts/apply-0049-calendar-schema-repair-staging.mjs` (new this round,
not wired into `package.json`, CI, or anything else -- committed purely

`drizzle/pending-review/` holds the migration itself). It has never been

in the environment and is a separate, explicit decision for the owner (or
an agent with the owner's explicit go-ahead for this specific action) to
make after reviewing this entry. In order, aborting immediately on any
failed check:
1. **Preflight**: asserts the config path is Staging's own
   (`wrangler.staging.jsonc`, `fundraising-os-staging-db`) and never
   mentions the production database name; hashes the migration file and
   refuses to proceed unless it matches `d029060`'s own exact, rehearsed

   -- a future edit to the `.sql` file without updating this constant (and
   re-rehearsing) is refused, not silently applied; confirms the
   Cloudflare credentials are present.
2. **Full recoverable backup before anything changes**: `wrangler d1
   export fundraising-os-staging-db --remote --config
   wrangler.staging.jsonc --output staging-backup-before-0049-<timestamp>.sql`,

3. **Before snapshot**: every row of `calendar_event_links` and
   `calendar_event_link_history`, via read-only `wrangler d1 execute
   --remote --command` queries.
4. **Applies the repair**: one single `db.batch()` call, built from the
   migration file's own parsed statements, against the REAL remote
   Staging D1 binding (`getPlatformProxy({configPath:
   "wrangler.staging.jsonc", remoteBindings: true})`) -- never `wrangler
   d1 execute --file`, whose cross-statement atomicity for a whole file is
   not reliably documented.
5. **After snapshot**: re-reads both tables and asserts
   `assert.deepEqual` against step 3's snapshot -- every row and column
   byte-for-byte unchanged.
6. **`PRAGMA foreign_key_check` and `PRAGMA integrity_check`**, both via
   `wrangler d1 execute --remote --command` directly against Staging (the
   CLI path, not the Worker binding, per the limitation above) -- must be
   clean and `"ok"` respectively.
7. **Schema-health check**: Staging's live schema, read via `SELECT
   name,type,tbl_name,sql FROM sqlite_schema ...`, through the same
   `compareSchemaObjects()`/`stagingSchemaObjects()` the Workspace Health
   page and `production-backup-readiness.test.mjs` already use -- must
   now report a clean match for both calendar tables, where it previously
   did not.
8. **Restore verification**: a SECOND full export (now schema-fixed),
   fed through this repo's own existing, proven

   scratch D1 database, restoring the fixed backup into it, and running

   recovery runbook requires, always deleting the scratch database
   afterward.

If any step fails, the script aborts immediately and prints which step
succeeded last and the exact command to restore the pre-repair backup.
Nothing in this plan touches `sqlite_schema` directly, nothing drops or
rebuilds a remote table outside of this one reviewed, rehearsed
migration, and nothing here is scheduled, automated, or self-triggering

### The headline finding: the apply script's own remote binding had a real gap

The review caught this before any remote mutation, from reading the
script alongside wrangler's own source, not from a CI failure:
`scripts/apply-0049-calendar-schema-repair-staging.mjs` called
`getPlatformProxy({remoteBindings: true})` against
`wrangler.staging.jsonc`, but that config's own `DB` binding never set
`"remote": true`. Confirmed directly in wrangler 4.92.0's bundled source
(`d1DatabaseEntry()`): a D1 binding only gets wired to the real remote
database when **both** `remoteBindings: true` is passed to
`getPlatformProxy()` **and** that specific binding's own config entry
also carries `remote: true` -- without the second half, the binding
silently falls back to an **empty, local, simulated** database while
every call still appears to succeed. Had this script actually been run
as written, it would have believed it repaired Staging while touching
nothing real at all. Fixed by adding `wrangler.staging-repair.jsonc`, a
dedicated, minimal config (the one D1 binding, `remote: true`, no other
bindings) used only by this repair's own scripts --
`wrangler.staging.jsonc`'s normal-development default is untouched.

### What this round built, one item per the review's own numbering

1. **Real target validation, offline-testable.**
   `lib/operations/staging-repair-target.ts` -- pure functions
   (`computeSchemaFingerprint`, `validateRepairTarget`) that cross-check
   the D1 binding's own live schema against an independently-fetched

   validated binding once and hands it back for the caller's own actual

2. **Concrete, rehearsed recovery -- not "import this file."**
   `lib/operations/calendar-schema-repair-recovery.ts` builds a real,

## 2026-10-19 (seventh follow-up review): two real bugs in the apply script's own verification/error-reporting logic, found by review and fixed with offline, injected-dependency regression tests -- repair SQL unchanged, nothing applied

**Scope of this round**: a second independent review of
`scripts/apply-0049-calendar-schema-repair-staging.mjs`, specifically its
pre-repair backup verification and its `reportFailure()` logic, after
the prior round's CI run (39285194523) had already passed cleanly. Two
concrete, named bugs, plus a related hardening request -- all in the
application script, not the repair SQL, which this review's own
instruction said to leave unchanged. **No remote mutation, deployment,
credentials used for actual remote execution, Google setup, Production
changes, or merge into `main` this round.**

### Bug 1: the pre-repair backup check compared node:sqlite rows against D1 rows with a prototype mismatch

`node:sqlite`'s own row objects have a **null prototype**
(`Object.getPrototypeOf(db.prepare(...).get())` is literally `null`),
while a D1 binding's `.all()` results are ordinary plain objects.
`assert.deepEqual` under `node:assert/strict` is `deepStrictEqual`,
which compares `[[Prototype]]` as part of equality -- so the Phase 3
backup-verification check (added last round: restore the pre-repair
export into an isolated `node:sqlite` database and compare its rows
against a fresh binding read) would have thrown on **every single run**,
even when the data matched exactly, purely because of the prototype
difference. Verified directly before fixing anything:

```
row: [Object: null prototype] { id: 'x', n: 5 }
deepEqual FAILED: Expected values to be strictly deep-equal
```

**Fixed**: `lib/operations/calendar-schema-repair-apply.ts`'s
`normalizeRow()`/`normalizeRows()` (`{...row}` spread -- preserves every
column's exact value and type, discards only the prototype) are now
applied to both sides of every row comparison in the script
(`snapshotCalendarTablesViaBinding()` and the new
`verifyBackupRestoresAndMatches()`). Regression test
(`tests/calendar-schema-repair-apply.test.mjs`) reproduces the bug
against a REAL `node:sqlite` row first (`assert.throws(() =>
assert.deepEqual(sqliteRow, d1ShapedRow))`), then proves the fix.

### Bug 2: reportFailure's fallback message contradicted itself for the one phase that actually tests row preservation

The previous round's `reportFailure()` had three branches: pre-repair
phases, the repair-batch phase, and a generic fallback for everything
else, with the fallback's own message claiming "the very next step
already confirmed every row... survived unchanged." `post-batch-row-check`
-- the phase that performs exactly that confirmation -- fell into this
SAME generic fallback when it failed, meaning a failure in the row-
preservation check itself produced a message asserting that check had
ALREADY PASSED. **Fixed**: `describeFailure()` now gives
`post-batch-row-check` its own explicit message -- the batch committed,
but preservation is **UNVERIFIED or MISMATCHED**, not confirmed either
way -- with the same read-only-inspection-first guidance as a genuinely
uncertain repair-batch failure, never a "no action needed" or "already
verified" claim. The underlying design flaw (an un-enumerated phase
silently inheriting the "already succeeded" message by falling through)
is also fixed structurally: phase classification is now two explicit
allowlists (`PRE_REPAIR_PHASES`, `POST_SUCCESS_VERIFICATION_PHASES|`),
and anything -- including a future, un-classified phase -- that doesn't
land in one of those or match `repair-batch`/`post-batch-row-check`
explicitly now defaults to **UNCERTAIN**, never to "already succeeded."

### Hardening: a bare `D1_ERROR` no longer counts as a confirmed rejection

`looksLikeCleanRejection()` previously matched on
`/SQLITE_CONSTRAINT|D1_ERROR|no such table|syntax error|FOREIGN KEY constraint/i`
-- but `D1_ERROR` is the generic wrapper prefix on **every** D1 failure,
including transient service faults and internal errors that prove
nothing about whether a write actually landed. Removed from the
alternation: only a message that also names a SPECIFIC, recognized
rejection cause (`SQLITE_CONSTRAINT`, `no such table`, `syntax error`,
`FOREIGN KEY constraint`) now counts as "clean." A bare
`D1_ERROR: Internal error` (or any other unrecognized D1 error) is now
correctly classified as UNCERTAIN, matching this round's own explicit
instruction: "An unknown D1 error must remain uncertain unless its
specific cause proves rejection."

### Refactor: the actual verification/error-reporting functions are now exercised with injected dependencies, no remote access

Per this round's own instruction, the fix is not just "normalize before
comparing" inline in the script -- the logic itself moved into
`lib/operations/calendar-schema-repair-apply.ts` (`PhaseError`,
`normalizeRow`/`normalizeRows`, `looksLikeCleanRejection`,
`snapshotCalendarTablesViaBinding`, `verifyBackupRestoresAndMatches`,
`describeFailure`), so the SAME functions the real script calls are
directly testable:
- `snapshotCalendarTablesViaBinding` takes the D1-like `db` as a
  parameter already -- tests inject a fake object with a scripted
  `.prepare().all()`, no real binding needed.
- `verifyBackupRestoresAndMatches` takes a `createSqliteDatabase`
  factory -- tests inject a real `node:sqlite` `DatabaseSync` (local,
  built-in, not "remote access") and hand-constructed D1-shaped plain

### The real bug a second review caught before any dispatch

The CI retention step (encrypt + upload both backups to the existing R2
bucket) used `set -uo pipefail` -- **missing `-e`**. A failed
`gzip`/`gpg`/`aws s3api put-object` would fall straight through to a
"Retained encrypted backup" **success** message and then
unconditionally `shred` every local copy -- silently and permanently
destroying the only recoverable backup on exactly the kind of failure
(a network blip, a wrong credential, a bucket typo) retention exists to
survive. This was caught by review, not by any test or CI run, before
the workflow was ever dispatched.

**Fixed** (commits `c2e7c20`, then `de172c9` re-pinning the job to it)
by moving the entire retention sequence out of CI shell script and into
tested, injectable-dependency application code:
- `lib/operations/calendar-schema-repair-apply.ts`'s `retainBackupSecurely()`
  checks compression, encryption, upload, and an INDEPENDENT remote
  read-back (byte-size verification via `aws s3api head-object`, never
  merely "the upload command exited zero") as four separate, explicit
  stages. Any failure returns `{ok: false, reason}` immediately; the
  original plaintext backup is removed ONLY once every stage, including
  verification, has explicitly succeeded.
- `applyRepairBatchGuardedByRetention()` is the structural checkpoint:
  `db.batch()` is literally unreachable in that function unless
  `retainPreRepairBackup()` first reports success -- not a convention a
  future edit could silently break.
- Two new `PhaseError` phases with their own `describeFailure()`
  messages: `pre-repair-retention` (nothing touched -- the mutation
  never ran) and `post-repair-retention` (the repair already succeeded
  and was already independently verified; this specific backup needs
  re-attempted retention, never a reason to revert).
- `scripts/lib/backup-retention.mjs` provides the real implementation
  (shelling out to the same `gzip`/`gpg`/`aws` tools and credentials the
  existing nightly-backup/monthly-restore-verify workflows already use);
  the old CI shell retention/cleanup steps were removed entirely.
- 17 new synthetic regression tests
  (`tests/calendar-schema-repair-apply.test.mjs`) inject a failure at
  exactly one stage (compression, encryption, upload, remote
  verification -- both thrown-error and returned-false forms) and
  assert `ok: false`, a specific reason, and -- the critical property --
  that the original backup file is NEVER shredded on any failure path;
  plus a direct proof that `db.batch()` is never invoked when pre-repair
  retention fails.
- `tests/backup-automation.test.mjs`'s own "the monthly verification job
  must not hold write access to the backup bucket" assertions
  (correctly) started failing once the new job was added to the same
  file -- rescoped to check the original `verify:` job's text
  specifically, plus a new, explicit, by-name assertion that ONLY the
  new, gated job holds the write credential.
- The job's `actions/checkout` pin was updated from the pre-fix commit
  to `c2e7c205b260d1cd068d90b0020b82ee9886e15` (the commit containing
  this fix) -- re-pinning any changed application code, per this
  round's own instruction, so a future dispatch actually runs the FIXED
  retention logic, not the vulnerable version the comments would
  otherwise describe.

correct as written; only `d1 info` was wrong.

`5f0ebf1`): removed `--remote` from the `d1 info` call. Extracted

builders in `scripts/lib/staging-repair-connect.mjs`, so the exact

spawning wrangler or touching the network at all. Target validation
itself is **not weakened** -- the same two-independent-path (binding +

## 2026-10-19 (tenth follow-up review): a second real dispatch hung for ~21 minutes after a failed remote-session startup -- diagnosed, fixed, still not applied; a likely permissions gap reported, not acted on

**Scope of this round**: the owner dispatched the (by-then `d1 info`-
fixed) repair job a second time -- run `39301756858`. It failed within
seconds, during the SAME read-only target-validation phase as before,
but this time the JOB itself did not end for ~21 minutes, until
GitHub's own 20-minute job-level timeout cancelled it. **Staging remains
completely unchanged -- the failure was during read-only target
validation, before any backup or mutation was ever attempted. No
recovery action was needed or taken. No token permission was broadened,
no credential was touched, the execution mechanism itself is unchanged,
no change to `main`, no OAuth, no live Google call, no merge.**

### What the actual run showed, inspected directly (job `118228469555`)

```
Opening the real remote Staging D1 binding (getPlatformProxy, remoteBindings: true)...
⎔ Establishing remote connection...
✘ [ERROR] A request to the Cloudflare API (/accounts/***/workers/subdomain/edge-preview) failed.
ABORTED during phase "target-validation": Failed to start the remote proxy session. There is likely additional logging output above.
Nothing on Staging was touched -- this failed before the repair batch was ever attempted. Fix the cause above and re-run; no recovery action of any kind is needed.
Error: The operation was canceled.
```
Step timing (via the Actions API, not estimated): the "Apply the
reviewed Calendar schema repair to Staging" step started at
`2026-10-19T18:21:23Z` and was marked `cancelled` at
`2026-10-19T18:42:35Z` -- **21 minutes 12 seconds**, even though the
error text above was already fully printed within the first few
seconds. The `verify` job on this SAME run independently confirmed
`skipped` (via the Actions API) -- the gated-dispatch mechanism itself
continues to work correctly; this round's defect is specifically the
HANG after a known, already-reported failure, not the gating or the
error-reporting logic (which fired exactly as designed, correctly
saying "nothing was touched").

### Diagnosis: a real, source-confirmed mechanism for the hang; a well-evidenced (not assumed) likely cause for the underlying failure

**The hang's mechanism, confirmed directly in wrangler 4.92.0's own
bundled source** (not guessed): `getPlatformProxy({remoteBindings:
true})` internally starts a real local Miniflare "proxy server worker"
(`startWorker(...)`), which itself must call Cloudflare's
`/accounts/{accountId}/workers/subdomain/edge-preview` API to obtain a
remote preview session. When that call fails, the worker's own `raw`
object emits an `"error"` event -- and the specific code path that then
throws `"Failed to start the remote proxy session. There is likely
additional logging output above."` does so **without disposing the
already-started local worker first**. The outer promise this agent's
code awaits rejects almost immediately (matching the observed timing:
the error text appeared within seconds), but the already-started local
Miniflare process/handle is left running, keeping Node's event loop
alive -- there is no object for OUR OWN code to dispose in this failure
(the rejection happens before `getPlatformProxy()` ever returns a
`proxy` at all), so this is a resource leak inside wrangler's own
error-handling path, not something fixable from this script's side
beyond forcing our own process to exit regardless.

**The likely cause of the underlying API failure -- reported as a
finding, not acted on.** Cross-referencing wrangler's own source (the
`edge-preview` endpoint is part of its temporary-preview-Worker/remote-
bindings machinery, structurally similar to deploying a short-lived
test Worker) against real-world reports:
- [cloudflare/workers-sdk#10091](https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/issues/10091) -- an open feature request confirming a token scoped for R2 bucket write access failed against this exact `edge-preview` endpoint, and only a broad `Workers Scripts: Edit` permission was found to work.
- A [Cloudflare community report](https://community.cloudflare.com/t/wrangler-edge-preview-minimum-permissions-free-plan-billing-and-token-revocation/968103) describes the SAME failure even with a token holding Individual Workers Editor plus account-wide Workers Content Read-only (`RemoteSessionAuthenticationError`, wrangler 4.148.0) -- Cloudflare has not documented the exact minimum permission set this feature needs, and it appears to require more than a narrowly D1-scoped token would plausibly have.

**Most likely cause, stated precisely, per this round's own
instruction**: the existing `CLOUDFLARE_D1_API_TOKEN` secret (named and,
by every use in this repo until now, scoped for D1 operations only --
`d1 info`/`d1 execute`/`d1 export`, all of which worked correctly in
every prior round's dispatch) most likely lacks the broader **Workers
Scripts: Edit** (account-level) permission that `getPlatformProxy({
remoteBindings: true})`'s own internal preview-session mechanism
requires. This is a well-evidenced, but **not certain**, diagnosis --
this agent has no Cloudflare dashboard access to directly inspect that
token's actual configured scope, and was explicitly instructed not to
assume the cause or broaden any permission itself. **If the owner wants
to confirm or resolve this**: check the `CLOUDFLARE_D1_API_TOKEN`
token's permission groups in the Cloudflare dashboard against `Account
> Workers Scripts > Edit`; if it is missing, either add it to the
existing token or provision a separate token with it for this specific
job. No such change was made or requested to be made by this agent.

### The fix made this round (addresses the hang, not the underlying cause)

Two changes, addressing two different failure modes, both in
`lib/operations/calendar-schema-repair-apply.ts` and wired into both
`scripts/apply-0049-calendar-schema-repair-staging.mjs` and
`scripts/recover-0049-calendar-schema-repair-staging.mjs` (both share
`connectAndValidateStagingTarget()`):
1. `withStartupTimeout()` wraps the `getPlatformProxy()` call with a
   bounded 90-second timeout -- defense-in-depth for a DIFFERENT,
   not-yet-observed failure mode (the promise never settling at all,
   rather than rejecting quickly as this one did). 3 new regression
   tests (resolves-before-timeout, rejects-before-timeout-with-the-
   real-error, times-out-with-its-own-message-if-the-promise-never-
   settles).
2. Both scripts now call `process.exit(0)`/`process.exit(1)` explicitly
   once `main()` has FULLY settled (including its own `finally { await
   dispose() }`), rather than relying on `process.exitCode` plus natural
   event-loop drain. This is the fix for the ACTUALLY observed hang:
   terminates the job promptly regardless of what a third-party
   dependency's internals left dangling.

**Target validation, the single-batch repair design, and every existing
backup/retention protection are unchanged** -- this round added
startup/shutdown robustness around the one call that failed; nothing
about what gets validated, how the repair is applied, or how backups
are retained was touched.

## 2026-10-19 (eleventh follow-up review): a bounded, read-only diagnostic mode added to capture the actual Cloudflare HTTP status/error code -- not dispatched

**Scope of this round**: the prior round's likely-permissions diagnosis was explicitly reported as evidenced-but-not-certain, based on OTHER users' reports, not this token's own actual failure. This round's instruction was to prepare a bounded, diagnostic-only mode -- one that attempts ONLY the target-validation connection and stops immediately after, never reaching backup export, repair, recovery, or scratch-database creation -- to capture the REAL HTTP status, Cloudflare API error code, and a sanitized error message from this token's own connection attempt, so a permission/auth rejection (401/403) can be told apart from a platform/session failure (5xx/gateway/retryable) before any remedy is decided. **Nothing was dispatched this round. Staging is completely unchanged. No token permission was broadened, no credential was substituted or viewed, the execution mechanism itself is unchanged, no change to `main`, no OAuth, no live Google call, no merge.**

### Answering "check whether Wrangler's existing diagnostic output exposes these before adding instrumentation": yes, confirmed via direct source inspection

Inspected wrangler 4.92.0's own bundled source directly (`node_modules/wrangler/wrangler-dist/cli.js`, `fetchResult`/`throwFetchError`/`APIError` around lines ~132960-133176 and the `ParseError`/`APIError` class definitions around lines ~3619-3674). A failed Cloudflare API call -- including the `edge-preview` call `getPlatformProxy({remoteBindings: true})` makes internally -- already throws an `APIError` object carrying:
- `.status` -- the real HTTP status code.
- `.code` -- Cloudflare's own numeric API error code, set from the response's `errors[0]?.code` when present.
- `.isGatewayError()` -- true for status `524`.
- `.isRetryable()` -- true whenever `String(status)` starts with `"5"`.
- `.accountTag` -- the account ID extracted from the request path. Not a secret, but **deliberately never surfaced by this round's diagnostics**, matching wrangler's own practice of redacting it as `***` in its console output and this round's instruction to never print environment/account details.

**No new instrumentation was added to wrangler itself.** This round's code only extracts and prints fields that already exist on the error object every prior failed dispatch already caught -- it was never read before because `describeFailure()` only ever printed `.message`.

### What was built

- `lib/operations/calendar-schema-repair-apply.ts`: `extractApiErrorDetails()` (walks an error's own `.cause` chain, bounded at depth 10 to avoid a cyclic chain looping forever, and returns `null` -- never a fabricated result -- when nothing in the chain has a numeric `.status`) and `classifyApiErrorDetails()` (401/403 → `likely-permission-or-auth`; 5xx/gateway/retryable → `likely-platform-or-session`; anything else, including `null` → `unclassified`, never guessing). 7 new regression tests using a hand-built `FakeApiError` mimicking wrangler's real shape -- including one proving `accountTag` is never included in the extracted result, and one proving the cyclic-`.cause`-chain case terminates. 37/37 tests pass in this file (30 pre-existing + 7 new).

## 2026-10-19 (twelfth follow-up review): the owner dispatched the diagnostic -- confirmed HTTP 403 / Cloudflare error code 10000, a permission/auth rejection, not a platform/session failure; owner steps provided, no action taken on the token

**Scope of this round**: the owner dispatched the new diagnostic mode -- run `39311943280` -- the first real use of it. **Staging remains completely unchanged**: the diagnostic job itself never attempts a backup, write, or scratch database, and both the `verify` and `apply-0049-calendar-schema-repair-staging` jobs on this same run independently confirm `skipped` (via the Actions API), proving the new mutual-exclusion gating worked exactly as designed on a real dispatch, not just in rehearsal. No token permission was changed, no credential was requested or viewed by this agent, no execution mechanism was altered.

### Evidence, inspected directly from the job's own log (job `118263511870`), not assumed

```
Diagnostic-only mode: attempting target validation (the SAME connection the real repair performs as its own first step), then stopping. No backup export, repair, recovery, or scratch database will be attempted, regardless of outcome.
Resolving the target database id via the wrangler CLI (d1 info)...
Reading the live schema via the wrangler CLI (read-only)...
Opening the real remote Staging D1 binding (getPlatformProxy, remoteBindings: true)...
⎔ Establishing remote connection...
✘ [ERROR] A request to the Cloudflare API (/accounts/***/workers/subdomain/edge-preview) failed.

Connection and/or target validation FAILED.
HTTP status: 403
Cloudflare API error code: 10000
isGatewayError(): false
isRetryable(): false
Sanitized error message: A request to the Cloudflare API (/accounts/***/workers/subdomain/edge-preview) failed.
Classification: likely-permission-or-auth -- a 401/403 means the token authenticated but was not allowed to do this specific thing -- consistent with the Workers Scripts permission gap reported in docs/AI-HANDOFF.md's prior round.
Nothing beyond this read-only connection attempt was performed. Staging is unchanged.
```
Both prior read-only steps -- `d1 info` (CLI) and the live schema read (CLI) -- printed no error at all; only the THIRD step, `getPlatformProxy({remoteBindings: true})`'s own internal preview-session call, failed. This matches the existing diagnosis exactly: the token authenticates fine and can do ordinary D1 operations, but is specifically rejected by the separate `edge-preview` endpoint remote bindings depends on.

**What a 403 + code 10000 means here.** Cloudflare's numeric error code `10000` is documented across many Cloudflare API endpoints simply as `"Authentication error"` -- a generic code Cloudflare reuses for several related-but-distinct situations (insufficient permissions, zone/account scope mismatch, IP restrictions, or an invalid/expired token), so the code alone does not pin down which. Combined with the HTTP status (`403`, not `401`) and this specific endpoint, the most consistent reading is: **the token is valid and authenticates successfully (a totally invalid/expired token would far more typically surface as `401`), but lacks a permission this specific endpoint requires** -- i.e. a genuine authorization/scope gap, not a platform or transient-session problem (confirmed structurally too: `isGatewayError()` and `isRetryable()` both report `false`, so retrying later would not plausibly help on its own).

This is now the token's **own, actual, confirmed** result -- no longer "other users' reports," which is exactly the distinction this round's instruction asked the diagnostic to establish.

### Owner steps: inspect the existing token's permissions

This agent has no Cloudflare dashboard access and cannot see which actual Cloudflare token the GitHub secret `CLOUDFLARE_D1_API_TOKEN` maps to -- GitHub secrets are write-only even to the repository owner once saved, so the token's identity and scope can only be checked at its source, in Cloudflare:
1. Sign in to the Cloudflare dashboard and go to **My Profile -> API Tokens** (`dash.cloudflare.com/profile/api-tokens`) -- or, if this token was created as an account-owned token rather than a user token, **Manage Account -> API Tokens** instead.
2. Find the token actually in use as the `CLOUDFLARE_D1_API_TOKEN` GitHub secret. If its identity isn't obvious from the token's name, cross-check by its "Last used" timestamp against a recent nightly backup or monthly verify run's timestamp (both already use this same secret successfully).
3. Click the token's "..." menu -> **Edit** (viewing a token's permissions does not require regenerating it) and review its **Permissions** list.
4. Specifically check for **Account > Workers Scripts > Edit**. Per the two independent reports already cited in the prior round's entry ([cloudflare/workers-sdk#10091](https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/issues/10091); a [Cloudflare community thread](https://community.cloudflare.com/t/wrangler-edge-preview-minimum-permissions-free-plan-billing-and-token-revocation/968103)), this is the permission the `edge-preview`/remote-bindings preview-session endpoint needs and that a narrowly D1-scoped token would not plausibly already have. **If it is absent, that is the confirmed cause of this 403.**

### Recommendation: a separate, short-lived repair token -- not a change to the existing backup/verify token

If `Account > Workers Scripts > Edit` is confirmed missing, this agent recommends **against** broadening the existing `CLOUDFLARE_D1_API_TOKEN` in place -- that token is also relied on, successfully and narrowly, by the nightly backup and monthly restore-verification jobs, and broadening it would widen what a leak of that one credential could do across all three jobs for no benefit to those other two. Instead:

- **Create a new, separate Cloudflare API token**, scoped to exactly:
  - **Account Resources**: Include -> this one specific Cloudflare account only (never "All accounts").
  - **Permissions**: `Account > D1 > Edit` (same as the existing token needs, for `d1 info`/`d1 execute`/`d1 export`) **plus** `Account > Workers Scripts > Edit` (the newly-required permission).
  - **Zone Resources**: none needed -- this repair is entirely account-level.
  - **TTL**: give it a short expiration (e.g. a few weeks), since it only needs to exist for the duration of this repair effort -- "short-lived" per this round's own instruction. A token nearing its TTL can simply be reissued if more time is needed; the expiration date only limits the *window* a leaked credential would remain useful, it does not limit how many times the token can be used within that window.
  - **Client IP Address Filtering**: optional. GitHub-hosted Actions runners use a large, changing IP range, so this is not usually practical to restrict for a GitHub-Actions-only token; most owners skip it for this reason.
- **Install it as its own, distinctly-named GitHub Actions secret** -- e.g. `CLOUDFLARE_D1_REPAIR_TOKEN` -- via this repository's **Settings -> Secrets and variables -> Actions -> New repository secret**, rather than overwriting the existing `CLOUDFLARE_D1_API_TOKEN` secret. (A GitHub **Environment** secret, tied to a protected environment that requires a manual approval step before a job can use it, is also worth considering as an extra gate, though not required.) Keeping it a separate secret name means the nightly backup and monthly verify jobs keep using the existing, narrower, already-proven token completely unchanged -- only the repair and diagnostic jobs would ever reference the new one.
- Once that new secret exists, wiring the `apply-0049-calendar-schema-repair-staging` and `diagnose-staging-connection` jobs' `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` env to reference it (in place of the current `secrets.CLOUDFLARE_D1_API_TOKEN`) is a small, mechanical workflow edit -- **not made this round**, since the token does not exist yet and this round's instruction was explicitly to recommend, not to request or change any credential. This agent will make that wiring change only on explicit future instruction, after the owner confirms the new token exists and its intended secret name.

**No token was requested in chat. No permission was changed. No credential was viewed or substituted by this agent.**

**No further repair dispatch, by this agent or otherwise recommended, until authorization is resolved and a diagnostic connection succeeds.** The diagnostic mode remains available to re-run (same instructions as above) once/if a new token is provisioned and wired in by the owner, to confirm the fix before ever attempting the repair job again. ## 2026-10-19 (closing this round): deployed-client review confirms a refresh failure cannot explain the reported error; live capture armed and exercised once more, clean; investigation paused, UNCONFIRMED

**Scope of this round**: reviewed the actually-deployed client code (`git show a0ccb2f:app/travel-planning/[id]/TripDashboardExperience.tsx`, the same confirmed-deployed commit as the prior correction) to check whether a failed page-data refresh, following a successful save, could produce the error banner the owner described. Then re-armed live, read-only network capture (a pass-through `window.fetch` wrapper logging URL path, method, timestamp, duration, status, and the `cf-ray` response header -- never altering any request/response) on the owner's own authenticated tab, and asked the owner to reproduce their next real action in it.

### Deployed-client review: a refresh failure cannot produce the displayed error banner

In the actually-deployed `TripDashboardExperience.tsx` (commit `a0ccb2f`, confirmed in the prior entry to be what's live):
- `function refresh() { router.refresh(); }` -- called, but **never awaited**, inside `withBusy()`: `try { await action(); refresh(); } catch (caught) { setError(...) }`.
- Because `refresh()` isn't awaited, a rejection from `router.refresh()`'s own internal page-data fetch cannot reach this `catch` block -- it is architecturally impossible for a failed refresh to populate `error` state through this path.
- The ONE place this component renders a visible error banner (`{error && <p className="travel-planning-error" role="alert">{error}</p>}`, line 197) only ever reflects a thrown error from the mutating `fetch()` call itself (the `PATCH`/`POST`/`DELETE` in `patchProspect`/`addDonor`/`removeDonor`), never from the background page-refresh.
- **Conclusion, corrected from two rounds ago**: the "a failed refresh gets misreported as a failed save" theory is also retracted. If the owner's banner literally read "Failed to fetch" (the browser's native message for a connection-level `fetch()` failure, not a non-2xx HTTP response), it can only have come from the mutating request itself failing at the network layer -- not from the separate, already-observed `.rsc` revalidation 503.

### Live capture: armed, exercised once, clean -- no failure this round

A sanitized, pass-through `window.fetch` wrapper was installed on the owner's own tab (already on the Teaneck trip page) logging path/method/timestamp/duration/status/`cf-ray` for every request, without altering any request or response. ## Trip Fundraising Totals -- Donor-Confirmation Correction (2026-10-20/21)

**STAGING ONLY. No Production deployment, no Production donor-record change, under this round.** Branch: `feature/independent-cloudflare-sandbox`.

### 1. The problem, and what was already there

Instructed: a pledge or donation confirmed during a trip must count toward the trip's fundraising results immediately, even before it is imported from JL, with no effect on the donor's financial account until that import happens.

Before touching anything, I reviewed the EXISTING Trip Fundraising Results Dashboard (2026-10-16, `drizzle/0046_trip_financial_attributions.sql`, `lib/relationships/trip-financial-attribution.ts`, `trips-data.ts`) and the general-CRM `pending_gift` category (pre-existing, Production-bound, `app/api/giving/pending/route.ts`) it reuses. This was a more capable starting point than a blank slate:

- A fundraiser can already record an unconfirmed `pending_gift`/`pending_pledge` from a trip and attribute it to the trip (`recordPendingGiftAndAttribute`/`recordPendingPledgeAndAttribute`), without creating any real financial transaction (`paid_cents`/`balance_cents` on these rows are always 0/committed-amount by construction, never touched by anything in this feature).
- `pending_gift` already has a full, reviewed JL-import reconciliation mechanism (`lib/giving/management.ts`'s `CONFIRM_PENDING_GIFT_SQL`/`pendingGiftMatches`, wired into `app/api/import/route.ts`): it requires an explicit fundraiser decision per candidate match, rejects an ambiguous pick, and rejects claiming one pending gift for two JL records. `pending_pledge` deliberately has NO such mechanism (documented as intentionally narrower, left for manual "Associate an existing pledge" instead).
- **The actual gap**: `countsInGivingTotals`/`summarizeTripFinancials` treated "pending" (not yet JL-imported) as synonymous with "unconfirmed" -- EVERY `pending_gift`/`pending_pledge`, including one the donor had explicitly confirmed on the trip, was excluded from every total and shown only as a generic "pending opportunity," exactly contrary to the task's core requirement. There was no field anywhere recording whether a pending entry was donor-confirmed.
- A second, related gap, surfaced by the task's own "collecting an existing pledge from before the trip must not be presented as a new commitment" requirement: "Associate an existing donation or pledge" let a fundraiser attribute ANY real giving_activities row to a trip, including an old, pre-existing pledge merely being serviced during the visit -- and `summarizeTripFinancials` counted every attributed pledge/gift as a new commitment unconditionally, with no way to say "this one isn't new."

Per instruction, I did **not** assume the existing `pending_gift`/`pending_pledge` rows on Staging were donor-confirmed, and did not touch any existing attribution's confirmation state. The screenshot's Rabbi & Mrs. Dovid Bashevkin $10,000 pending donation does **not currently exist as a row on Staging** (confirmed by direct query -- see Verification, below -- Staging currently has zero trips at all); it was not touched, and could not have been, by anything in this round. The migration's defaults (below) guarantee that if/when such a record exists anywhere, its confirmation status is never changed by the migration itself.

### 2. Design

**New migration**: `drizzle/0050_trip_attribution_confirmation.sql` -- four new, additive columns on the EXISTING `trip_financial_attributions` table only (same precedent as `giving_activities.confirmed_by_activity_id`, `drizzle/0016`: plain `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN`, no FK clause). No existing table, column, index, or row changes.

- `donor_confirmed_at` (nullable integer): NULL = unconfirmed opportunity (every existing row's only possible value, since the column didn't exist before). Non-null = a fundraiser has explicitly recorded the donor's confirmation. Only meaningful while the attribution's underlying (possibly JL-merge-resolved) category is still `pending_gift`/`pending_pledge` -- an already-real category is already confirmed by JL itself.
- `commitment_kind` (`'new_commitment'` default | `'preexisting_pledge_collection'`): defaults `'new_commitment'` for every existing and new row unless explicitly set otherwise -- zero behavior change for anything attributed before this round. Settable to `'preexisting_pledge_collection'` only on an already-real (already-JL) category -- enforced in `attributeGivingActivityToTrip`, since a record that doesn't exist in JL yet cannot be "pre-existing."
- `reported_cash_collected_cents` (nullable integer): a fundraiser-reported, trip-scoped cash figure, used only for `preexisting_pledge_collection` attributions. Deliberately **never** read from or written to the underlying pledge's own `paid_cents` (that is a lifetime cumulative total that would misattribute money paid before the trip as if collected during it) -- a structurally separate, trip-reported fact, distinguished from the JL-recorded figure everywhere it's shown.
- `reconciled_pending_attribution_id` (nullable text, no DB-level FK, same precedent): set on a NEW attribution of a real record when that same write also retires an existing pending attribution for the same trip+donor -- audit/display only.

**Numbering**: `drizzle/pending-review/0049_fix_calendar_schema_text_staging_repair.sql` already reserves "0049" for a separate, unrelated, not-yet-reviewed draft kept outside `drizzle/` for exactly that reason. This migration is `0050`, continuing the real sequence directly after `0048`, so it can never collide with that draft if it's later renumbered in. `lib/data-health/production-baseline.ts`'s hardcoded migration count was bumped 49 -> 50 and `production-baseline/schema-manifest.json` regenerated (`node scripts/generate-production-baseline.mjs --write`), following the exact same routine maintenance step prior rounds did for 0045-0048.

**Logic** (`lib/relationships/trip-financial-attribution.ts`'s `summarizeTripFinancials`, rewritten; `lib/relationships/trips-data.ts`, extended):

- A `pending_gift`/`pending_pledge` with `donorConfirmedAt` set now counts immediately: a confirmed pledge counts its full committed amount toward "new pledges secured" with its full amount as a provisional, "awaiting JL" outstanding balance (nothing paid pre-JL by construction); a confirmed gift counts its full amount toward "new donations secured" AND as cash collected "awaiting JL" (a gift has no partial-payment concept -- it's reported received in full, just not yet JL-recorded).
- Still-unconfirmed `pending_gift`/`pending_pledge` rows are **excluded** from every confirmed total exactly as before, now labeled "Unconfirmed opportunity," never "Awaiting JL."
- `TripFinancialSummary` now exposes the split the task's own requirement 4 calls for: `cashCollectedRecordedInJlCents` vs. `cashCollectedAwaitingJlCents` (sum = `cashCollectedCents`, kept for the top-line figure), `outstandingBalanceRecordedInJlCents` vs. `outstandingBalanceAwaitingJlCents` (sum = `outstandingCommittedBalanceCents`), plus `preexistingPledgeCollectionCashCents` and `awaitingJlCount`.
- `commitmentKind === "preexisting_pledge_collection"` is **excluded unconditionally** from every "new commitment" figure (committed/pledge/donation counts, outstanding balance), regardless of its own category or confirmation state -- only its own `reportedCashCollectedCents` ever counts, and only as cash collected.
- **Ambiguous-match guard** (`attributeGivingActivityToTrip`): attributing a REAL (already-JL) record now looks up every still-active, not-yet-JL (`pending_gift`/`pending_pledge`, including an already-confirmed one) attribution for the SAME donor on the SAME trip (`listReconcilableTripAttributions`). If one or more exist, the caller MUST explicitly pass which one (if any) this record reconciles -- `"none"` for "this is a deliberate, separate, additional commitment," a specific attribution id to reconcile it, or the call is rejected with `reason: "reconciliation_choice_required"` and the exact candidate list attached, never auto-picked by donor+amount. A chosen reconciliation retires the old pending attribution (`removed_at`, `removed_reason: "Reconciled with JL-imported record"`) in the SAME atomic D1 batch as the new attribution's insert -- never a moment where both are active (double-counted) or both removed (the commitment silently vanishes). This is a NEW, trip-scoped mechanism, independent of (and never touching) the general JL-import pipeline -- `pending_gift`'s own existing, separately-reviewed auto-merge reconciliation (`CONFIRM_PENDING_GIFT_SQL`) is completely untouched and keeps working exactly as before; this new mechanism is what closes the gap for `pending_pledge`, which never had any reconciliation path at all, and also catches a fundraiser manually re-attributing a `pending_gift`'s own real JL record as a separate (would-be duplicate) attribution.
- **`confirmTripAttribution`/`unconfirmTripAttribution`** (new): marks (or un-marks, to correct a mistake) an EXISTING attribution donor-confirmed, WITHOUT recreating it -- the task's own explicit requirement. Idempotent; restricted to attributions whose resolved category is still `pending_gift`/`pending_pledge` (`reason: "not_applicable"` otherwise, since JL's own confirmation already speaks for a real category). Exposed via a new `PATCH` on `app/api/trips/[id]/prospects/[prospectId]/attributions/[attributionId]/route.ts` (`{ donorConfirmed: true|false }`).
- **Recording a new pledge/gift from a trip** (`recordPendingGiftAndAttribute`/`recordPendingPledgeAndAttribute`) now accepts an explicit `confirmed` boolean from the fundraiser at the moment of recording (never defaulted to true) -- set via a new UI checkbox, "The donor confirmed this donation/pledge."

**UI** (`app/travel-planning/[id]/TripDashboardExperience.tsx`): the "Record a new donation/pledge" panel gained the confirmation checkbox with updated hint text distinguishing "counted immediately, labeled Awaiting JL" from "stays an unconfirmed opportunity." The "Associate an existing donation or pledge" panel gained a "secured on this trip" vs. "pre-existing pledge, just collecting/linking now" choice (shown only for a selected real-category record), a trip-reported cash input for the latter, and -- when reconcilable candidates exist for that donor -- a required radio choice naming each candidate or "a separate, additional commitment." Each attributed row shows a "Mark donor-confirmed"/"Unconfirm" toggle for a still-pending entry, and a pre-existing-collection row is labeled distinctly from its own JL-recorded lifetime figures. The trip summary now shows "recorded in JL" / "awaiting JL" sublabels on Cash Collected and Outstanding Balance, and splits the bottom list into "Unconfirmed opportunities" (excluded above) and "Donor-confirmed, awaiting JL" (already counted above, shown for transparency).

Everywhere, the underlying `giving_activities` row's own `committed_cents`/`paid_cents`/`balance_cents` are never written by any of this -- re-confirmed by the same `UPDATE giving_activities SET...(committed_cents|paid_cents|balance_cents)` source-inspection guard the existing tests already enforced, now re-run against this round's additions too.

## Trip Fundraising Totals -- Reconciliation Concurrency Fix, Real-Execution Tests, Main-Sync Investigation, Label Fix (2026-10-21)

**STAGING ONLY. No Production deployment, no Production donor-record change, under this round. Independent review requested; stopping here per instruction.** Branch: `feature/independent-cloudflare-sandbox`, building on commit `3ac6097`.

### 1. Reconciliation concurrency gap -- fixed

**The real defect, confirmed first, not assumed**: `attributeGivingActivityToTrip` read `listReconcilableTripAttributions` candidates, then wrote the new attribution and retired the chosen pending one in one D1 **batch** -- which guarantees those two statements commit or fail TOGETHER, but does nothing to stop the READ itself from going stale before the WRITE runs. I reproduced the exact scenario described: reverted `trips-data.ts` to commit `3ac6097`'s own version (temporarily, locally, never pushed) and ran two concurrent real calls (via the new real-execution test harness, see Section 2) against the SAME pending attribution with two different real records. Both succeeded, producing **two active attributions for one $15,000 commitment -- a real, reproduced $30,000 double-count.** That reproduction is preserved as the "before" half of the regression test.

**The fix -- two database-enforced mechanisms, together, not one alone** (confirmed the existing giving_activity_id unique index, `drizzle/0046`, does not cover this at all -- it only prevents the same giving_activities row being double-attributed, never two DIFFERENT real records racing for the same reconciliation target):

1. **`drizzle/0051_trip_reconciliation_concurrency_guard.sql`** -- one new partial UNIQUE index, `trip_financial_attributions_active_reconciled_pending_uidx`, on `(reconciled_pending_attribution_id) WHERE removed_at IS NULL AND reconciled_pending_attribution_id IS NOT NULL`. At most one ACTIVE attribution can ever claim to reconcile a given pending id -- a real, structural guarantee, same enforcement level as the existing giving-activity-id index.
2. **`attributeGivingActivityToTrip`'s INSERT is now conditional**: `INSERT INTO trip_financial_attributions (...) SELECT ... WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM trip_financial_attributions WHERE id = ? AND removed_at IS NULL)`, re-checking the chosen target is STILL active fresh inside the SAME transaction as the retiring UPDATE -- never trusting the earlier, separate read. If the target vanished for ANY reason (a competing reconciliation, or an unrelated ordinary removal) between the read and this write, the INSERT itself inserts zero rows (checked via `results[0].meta.changes` after the batch, same established pattern as `trips-data.ts`'s own `scheduleProspectMeeting`), and the call fails cleanly with `reconciliation_target_not_found` -- nothing is left to clean up.
3. **A second, independent logic bug in the same function, found while fixing this**: the explicit-reconciliation-choice handling was gated on `if (candidates.length > 0)` -- so a caller's explicit, specific `reconcilesAttributionId` silently fell through to "treat as a separate, additional commitment" the moment candidates had already emptied out (e.g. the chosen target had just been reconciled or removed by someone else). Fixed by checking the caller's own explicit choice FIRST, independent of how many candidates currently exist -- an explicitly-named target that isn't among the freshly-read candidates is now always rejected, never silently reinterpreted.
4. The `catch` block now distinguishes a UNIQUE violation on the new index (`isReconciledPendingUniqueViolation`, matching `trip_financial_attributions.reconciled_pending_attribution_id` in the thrown error's own message) from the unrelated `already_attributed` case, reporting `reconciliation_target_not_found` for the former -- the two are different failures with different causes and must not share one label.

### 2. Real behavioral regression tests -- a new testing capability for this codebase

Every prior trip-financial-attribution test in this codebase exercises either a pure function directly, or a hand-copied reproduction of the real SQL/source text -- documented, repeatedly, as the only option, since every D1-touching module imports `"cloudflare:workers"` and "cannot run outside a Workers runtime at all." A hand-copied reproduction cannot prove a concurrency fix is real; it can only prove the copy behaves as the person typing it expected, which is exactly the blind spot a race condition hides in. This round adds the infrastructure to go further, used only for this one file so far:

- **`tests/helpers/cloudflare-workers-shim-loader.mjs`** + **`cloudflare-workers-shim.mjs`**: a Node module-customization hook (`module.register`) that intercepts the `"cloudflare:workers"` specifier (which does not exist outside an actual Workers runtime) and resolves it to a tiny virtual module exporting a mutable `env` object a test sets `env.DB` on. The same loader also retries a failed relative-specifier resolution with `.ts` appended, since this codebase's own `.ts` files import siblings by their bare, extensionless name (the vinext/Vite bundler this app ships with resolves that; plain Node's ESM resolver does not) -- zero production source files changed to make this work.
- **`tests/helpers/d1-sqlite-adapter.mjs`**: a minimal `D1Database`-shaped adapter over `node:sqlite`'s real `DatabaseSync`, implementing exactly the subset this codebase's write paths use (`prepare().bind().first()/.all()/.run()`, and `.batch()` as one real transaction -- commits or rolls back and rethrows together, matching D1's own documented all-or-nothing semantics).
- **`tests/trip-reconciliation-concurrency.test.mjs`**: calls the REAL, unmodified `attributeGivingActivityToTrip`/`listReconcilableTripAttributions`/`removeTripFinancialAttribution`/`listTripFinancialAttributions`/`summarizeTripFinancials` from `lib/relationships/trips-data.ts` and `trip-financial-attribution.ts`, against a real, in-memory database built from every real, committed migration in order (same rigor as `trip-financial-attribution-schema.test.mjs`, but calling the actual production functions instead of reproducing their SQL). Covers, with the real DB state checked after each, not just the function's own return value:
  - **Two competing real records claiming the same pending entry** (`Promise.all` of two real calls) -- exactly one succeeds, the other fails with `reconciliation_target_not_found`, exactly one active attribution exists afterward, the pending entry is retired exactly once, the commitment counts exactly once ($15,000, never $0 or $30,000), and the losing request's own giving-activities row has no attribution row at all, active or removed.
  - **A repeated request** (the exact same call sent twice, sequentially) -- the second fails as a stale target, attribution state is byte-for-byte unchanged (`assert.deepEqual` against the pre-retry snapshot).
  - **A stale reconciliation target** -- the pending entry removed for an ORDINARY, unrelated reason (`removeTripFinancialAttribution`, nothing to do with reconciliation) before the call; candidates confirmed genuinely empty; the explicit, now-stale `reconcilesAttributionId` is still rejected, never silently treated as a separate commitment just because candidates is empty.
  - **A legitimate, explicitly separate commitment** (`reconcilesAttributionId: "none"`) still succeeds correctly while an unrelated pending entry for the same donor remains untouched and active.
- **Proven to actually catch the original bug, not merely pass by construction**: ran this exact test file three ways -- (a) fixed code + fixed migrations: all pass; (b) commit `3ac6097`'s own `trips-data.ts` + the new migration: the race is closed (the index alone already prevents the double-insert) but the reported failure reason is the wrong, misleading `already_attributed`, caught by the test; (c) commit `3ac6097`'s `trips-data.ts` + migration `0051` removed entirely: **the real, reproduced double-count** described above. Both (b) and (c) were run as literal verification steps, not asserted from memory.
- `tests/trip-financial-attribution.test.mjs`'s own prior source-inspection assertions for this guard were updated (window sizes widened to the real, measured character distances; the stale "must be gated on candidates.length" check replaced with the correct independent-of-candidates-length check; the "atomic batch" structural assertion replaced with one matching the new conditional-INSERT shape) and now explicitly point to the real-execution test above as the actual proof, not a redundant restatement of it.
- Registered in `scripts/run-tests.mjs`'s `TEST_FILES`.

### 5. Summary-label fix -- `awaitingJlCount` split by category

**The bug, confirmed by reading the code, not assumed**: `summarizeTripFinancials` incremented one shared `awaitingJlCount` for EVERY donor-confirmed, not-yet-JL record -- both pledges and gifts -- and the UI's "New pledges secured" card displayed that same combined number as its own "N awaiting JL" sublabel. A donor-confirmed donation sitting on the same trip as a donor-confirmed pledge would inflate the pledge card's own count (e.g. 1 pledge + 1 donation both awaiting JL reported "2 awaiting JL" on the pledge card, which has exactly one).

**Fix**: `TripFinancialSummary.awaitingJlCount` replaced with `awaitingJlPledgeCount`/`awaitingJlDonationCount`, incremented in the already-existing pledge/gift branch split inside `summarizeTripFinancials` (no new branching logic needed -- the split point already existed for `newPledgesSecuredCents`/`newDonationsSecuredCents`). `TripDashboardExperience.tsx`'s "New pledges secured" card now reads `awaitingJlPledgeCount`; the "New donations secured" card gained the same, previously-missing, category-correct sublabel (`awaitingJlDonationCount`) for symmetry -- the task named only the pledge card's defect, but the donation card had the identical class of bug latent (it just happened to read nothing at all before, rather than an inflated number, since no field existed for it).

**New regression test** (`trip-financial-attribution.test.mjs`): a trip with exactly one donor-confirmed pledge AND one donor-confirmed donation asserts `awaitingJlPledgeCount === 1` and `awaitingJlDonationCount === 1` -- explicitly never 2 on either side. The three pre-existing tests that asserted the old combined field were updated to assert the correct category-specific one for their own scenario, plus an explicit assertion that the OTHER category's count is 0 (a donation test now also asserts `awaitingJlPledgeCount === 0`, and vice versa) -- catching exactly the inflation bug being fixed, not just the field rename.
